lines: A widening frontier is good at one thing: telling you the fewest steps to somewhere.
It has nothing useful to say when the real structure is a dependency, or a cluster that can only reach itself. For that you need to go the other way entirely.
Push one path as deep as it will go, before you ever try anything else.
Here's an edge pointing from some vertex straight back to one of its own ancestors, still sitting on the current path.
What kind of edge is that?
answer: A back edge. And that alone already means there's a cycle.
The ancestor can already reach this vertex going forward, through the tree. The back edge just closes the loop.

lines: Give every vertex two numbers: when it was first found, and when the search finished exploring everything underneath it.
Take any two vertices and look at those two ranges. They're either completely separate from each other, or one sits entirely inside the other.
They can never partly overlap. And whenever one range nests fully inside another, that's exactly when one vertex is a true descendant of the other.
A tree edge is simply part of the search tree itself.
A back edge points up to an ancestor, and that's what closes a cycle.
A forward edge points down to something already fully finished.
Everything else — a different branch entirely, maybe even a different starting point — that's a cross edge.
All four of those come straight out of comparing two numbers per vertex. Nothing else is needed.
Every edge in an undirected graph eventually gets walked from both of its ends.
So can its search ever produce a forward edge, or a cross edge, the way a directed one can?
answer: No — only tree and back edges are possible.

A forward edge would need that same connection to already exist from the other direction, which forces it to be a back edge instead. A cross edge would need two separate branches, and an undirected graph's own edges rule that out.

lines: In a directed graph, a cycle shows up the moment the search finds an edge to a vertex still actively being explored right now.
An undirected graph doesn't even need that bookkeeping. If you bump into a vertex you've already visited, and it isn't the one you just came from, that's already a cycle.
The two tests look different because an undirected search can never produce that third kind of edge, the one that would otherwise confuse things.
Write the search the natural, recursive way, and point it at a dependency chain a few hundred thousand steps long.
It crashes. Not because the logic is wrong, but because every one of those nested calls has to live somewhere, and the language's own call stack runs out of room.
Swap that call stack for one you manage yourself, and the exact same search finishes, visiting every single one of those vertices, no crash at all.
Run this same search on a graph with no cycle anywhere, and something falls out almost for free.
Read off the order vertices finished in, reversed, and you already have an order where nothing comes before something it depends on.
That's not a new algorithm. It's the traversal you just built, read a particular way.
